finding_key: packages/frontend/src/app/slides/pptx-actions.ts::new pptx export path feeds unvalidated, document-controlled image `src` into a credentialed fetch, then embeds the response bytes into the downloaded artifact
evidence: The mechanics the claim describes are all present in the supplied code: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` (pptx-actions.ts:88-100) hands every deck image `src` to `docsImageFetcher`, which does `fetch(resolveImageUrl(url), { credentials: "include" })` with no scheme/host allowlist (export-utils.ts:12-18, 46-56), and `exportPptx` writes the returned bytes verbatim into `ppt/media/imageN.{ext}` with `extFromMime` defaulting to `png` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts, Step 2 / `extFromMime`). `ImageElement.data.src` is free-form `string` in the model and the backend content PUT validator only checks element `id`/`type`/`frame` (docs-content.controller.ts `assertValidElement`), so a collaborator or API caller can plant an arbitrary URL. Two caveats reduce the impact from what the prose claims: a default-mode `fetch` to a non-CORS cross-origin/LAN host will have its response blocked (request is still issued, so blind SSRF/pixel-tracking holds, but its body cannot be embedded), so byte exfiltration is limited to origins that grant credentialed CORS to the frontend (i.e. the app's own backend); and the same unvalidated-src → credentialed-fetch → embed-bytes pattern already exists in the docs DOCX/PDF exporters, which the reviewer acknowledges. Net: the defect as described is real, though it needs write access to the deck plus the victim exporting and sharing the file.
